passages.t: Blessing again, and the worth of a life
passages.happening:
God blesses Noah and his sons with the first blessing again: “Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth” (verse 1). The animals will now fear people (verse 2).

Then God gives something new. “Everything that lives and moves will be food for you; just as I gave you the green plants, I now give you all things” (verse 3). But there is one limit: “you must not eat meat with its lifeblood still in it” (verse 4).

God says he will require an accounting for every human life that is taken (verse 5). “Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man his blood will be shed; for in His own image God has made mankind” (verse 6). And again: be fruitful and multiply (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
This is a new start, and it sounds like Genesis 1. The same blessing, the same command to fill the earth. But the world is different now. In chapter 1 God gave people plants for food (1:29). Now he allows meat, and fear comes between people and animals. The world after the flood is a world with blood in it.

So God sets limits on blood. People may eat animals, but not with the blood, because the blood stands for the life, and life belongs to God. Israel's law said it plainly: “the life of the flesh is in the blood” (Leviticus 17:11). Draining the blood was a way of saying: this life was God's gift, not mine to take as I please.

And human blood is in a class of its own. The reason is given: ‘in His own image God has made mankind’. To kill a person is to strike at the image of God. Chapter 6 said the earth was full of violence. Now, before the new world begins, God draws a line around every human life.

Later Jewish teachers, in the Talmud, spoke of seven laws given to all the descendants of Noah, that is, to every nation. Among them are the bans on murder and on eating flesh torn from a living animal. They drew most of the seven from passages in Genesis.
passages.later:
The early church remembered the ban on blood. When the apostles decided what to ask of Gentile believers, they included abstaining “from blood” (Acts 15:20).

The Bible goes on to say that blood makes atonement, that is, it covers sin and restores people to God (Leviticus 17:11). Jesus takes up that language at his last supper: “This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins” (Matthew 26:28).

The image of God remains a reason to honor every person, even in how we speak. James says we curse people “who have been made in God’s likeness” (James 3:9).
passages.hard:
Does verse 6 command the death penalty? Christians differ.

Many hold that it does. They point out that the verse comes long before the law of Moses, and is spoken to Noah, the father of every nation. On this view it gives governments a lasting duty to punish murder with death, and the reason is not revenge but the worth of the life that was taken. Paul says the ruler “does not carry the sword in vain” (Romans 13:4).

Many others read it differently. Some take the verse as describing what will follow from violence, more like a proverb than a law. Others read it as a principle, that murder deserves the gravest answer because life is sacred, without requiring every state in every age to take a life. Some point out that God himself protected Cain (4:15), and that the Bible's line around human life is a reason to be very slow to take one.

Christians differ, and these notes do not settle it. What every side agrees on is the verse's own reason: every human being is made in God's image, and every human life is precious to God.
passages.asks: God draws a line around every human life ‘for in His own image God has made mankind’. Ask whose life you treat as cheap, in what you say, what you watch or what you ignore. Then ask what it would look like to honor God's image in the person you least want to.

passages.t: The covenant and the bow in the clouds
passages.happening:
God speaks to Noah and his sons: “Behold, I now establish My covenant with you and your descendants after you” (verse 9). The covenant is also with every living creature that came out of the ark: birds, livestock and wild animals (verse 10).

The promise is plain: “Never again will all life be cut off by the waters of a flood; never again will there be a flood to destroy the earth” (verse 11).

God gives a sign. “I have set My rainbow in the clouds, and it will be a sign of the covenant between Me and the earth” (verse 13). Whenever the rainbow appears, God says, “I will remember My covenant” (verse 15). He repeats it: “I will see it and remember the everlasting covenant” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
A covenant is a binding promise that creates a lasting bond. Many covenants in the ancient world had two sides, with duties for each. This one is different. God makes all the promises. Noah does nothing to earn it, and nothing can break it. It is given to ‘all generations to come’ (verse 12), and to the animals as well as to people.

Count the word ‘covenant’ in these verses: it comes again and again, like a bell. The slow repetition sounds like a solemn promise read aloud.

The Hebrew word for rainbow, qeshet, is the ordinary word for a bow, the weapon of a soldier or a hunter. Some readers see a picture here: after the storm of judgment, God hangs up his war bow in the sky. The text does not say this, but it fits.

And notice who the sign is for. Most signs are for people. This one, first of all, is for God: ‘I will see it and remember’. Every rainbow is God's own reminder of his promise. People who see it can know he is remembering.
passages.later:
The prophets lean on this promise. God says to his people, “I swore that the waters of Noah would never again cover the earth. So I have sworn that I will not be angry with you or rebuke you” (Isaiah 54:9). And then: “Though the mountains may be removed and the hills may be shaken, My loving devotion will not depart from you, and My covenant of peace will not be broken” (Isaiah 54:10).

Hosea promises a day when God will make “a covenant for them with the beasts of the field” and will “abolish bow and sword and weapons of war” (Hosea 2:18).

The rainbow appears around God's throne. Ezekiel sees brilliant light around God “like that of a rainbow in a cloud on a rainy day” (Ezekiel 1:28). John sees “a rainbow that gleamed like an emerald encircled the throne” (Revelation 4:3). The sign of mercy after judgment surrounds the one who rules all things.
passages.hard: A word for anyone who has lived through a flood, a storm or another disaster. God's promise is that there will never again be a flood to destroy all life. It is not a promise that no one will ever suffer a flood. Floods and storms still come, and they still take homes and lives. The Bible does not tell you that your loss was a punishment. When Jesus was asked about people killed when a tower fell, he asked, “Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you” (Luke 13:4-5). If you are carrying grief or fear from a disaster, you need people with you, not only answers. Please talk with someone you trust, and the Find Help page has people you can call.
passages.asks: God bound himself by a promise he would never break, and set a sign in the sky to remember it. Ask which of God's promises you find hardest to believe. The next time you see a rainbow, let it ask you whether you trust the God who remembers.

passages.happening:
Noah's sons who came out of the ark were Shem, Ham and Japheth. The text adds, “And Ham was the father of Canaan” (verse 18). From these three the whole earth was filled (verse 19).

Noah, “a man of the soil”, plants a vineyard (verse 20). He drinks some of the wine, gets drunk, and lies uncovered in his tent (verse 21).

Ham sees his father's nakedness and goes out and tells his two brothers (verse 22). Shem and Japheth take a garment, lay it across their shoulders, and walk in backward. They cover their father without looking at him (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
The story sounds like the garden again. A man of the soil, a plant, its fruit, nakedness and shame, then a covering. The new world has the old problem. Even Noah, the righteous man who walked with God, falls.

The Bible tells this without excusing Noah. Genesis often reports what people do and lets the story show the results. It does not hide the failures of its heroes.

In the ancient world a father's honor was closely guarded. To expose or mock your father was a grave offense. Ham does not cover his father; he tells. His brothers go to great lengths not to see their father's shame. They walk backward, faces turned away, and cover him.

Notice that verse 18 mentions Canaan before anything happens. The writer wants the reader to remember who Canaan's father is. Canaan was the ancestor of the peoples who lived in the land later promised to Abraham, and Israel's first hearers knew them well.
passages.later:
The Bible says much about drunkenness after this. “Wine is a mocker, strong drink is a brawler, and whoever is led astray by them is not wise” (Proverbs 20:1). Paul says, “Do not get drunk on wine, which leads to reckless indiscretion. Instead, be filled with the Spirit” (Ephesians 5:18).

What Shem and Japheth do is what love does in the New Testament. “Hatred stirs up dissension, but love covers all transgressions” (Proverbs 10:12). Peter repeats it: “love covers over a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4:8). Covering here does not mean pretending nothing happened. It means refusing to make another's shame into a show.
passages.hard:
What exactly did Ham do? The text says he ‘saw his father's nakedness’ and told his brothers. It does not say more, and readers have long asked whether there was more.

The plain reading takes the words as they stand. Ham looked on his father's shame and made it known, perhaps mocking him. In a world built on honor, that was a deep wrong.

Some ancient Jewish teachers, and some modern scholars, think the words hide a worse act. They note that Leviticus uses similar language about ‘nakedness’ for forbidden sexual acts, and that verse 24 says Noah learned what Ham ‘had done to him’. On this reading Ham did something shameful to his father, not only saw him.

Others, among them some ancient rabbis, thought Canaan himself had a part in it, which would help explain why the curse falls on him.

The text does not settle it, and these notes do not either. What it shows clearly is the contrast: one son exposed his father's shame, and two sons covered it.
passages.asks: Two brothers walked backward to cover their father's shame. Ask what you do when you see someone else's failure: do you tell it, or cover it? Then ask the harder question. Where are you, like Noah, living after a great rescue and still falling in the same old ways?

passages.t: Canaan cursed, and the death of Noah
passages.happening:
Noah wakes from his drunkenness and learns what his youngest son had done to him (verse 24). He says, “Cursed be Canaan! A servant of servants shall he be to his brothers” (verse 25).

He blesses the God of Shem: “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Shem! May Canaan be the servant of Shem” (verse 26). And he prays that God will give Japheth room, that Japheth may “dwell in the tents of Shem, and may Canaan be his servant” (verse 27).

Noah lives 350 years after the flood. “So Noah lived a total of 950 years, and then he died” (verses 28-29).
passages.hearers:
Notice who speaks the curse. It is Noah, not God. In this chapter God speaks blessing and covenant. The curse comes from a man waking from drunkenness and shame.

Notice who is cursed. It is Canaan, Ham's son, not Ham. The text does not say why. Some readers think the son suffers for what his father did, a son who shamed his father being shamed through his own son. Others think Canaan was somehow involved. Others read Noah's words as looking ahead to the later history of the Canaanites, which Israel's first hearers knew.

The first hearers would hear the names as peoples. Shem was the ancestor of Abraham's family (11:10-26). The word ‘Semitic’ comes from his name. Japheth was linked with peoples to the north and west. Canaan was the ancestor of the peoples in the land God promised to Abraham. Israel later made some Canaanites, the people of Gibeon, servants at God's house: “you are under a curse and will perpetually serve as woodcutters and water carriers” (Joshua 9:23).

The last words are the old refrain of chapter 5: ‘and then he died’. Noah came through the flood, but not through death.
passages.later:
The Bible does not say a curse passes on forever from parents to children by birth. Ezekiel says, “A son will not bear the iniquity of his father, and a father will not bear the iniquity of his son” (Ezekiel 18:20). And Canaanites themselves were welcomed. Rahab of Jericho, a Canaanite, is named in the family line of Jesus (Matthew 1:5). A Canaanite woman begs Jesus for her daughter, and he praises her great faith (Matthew 15:22-28).

Paul says God “made every nation of men” from one man (Acts 17:26), and that in Christ “There is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28). The Bible's last picture is “a multitude too large to count, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue” (Revelation 7:9).
passages.hard:
Noah's words were spoken over Canaan, a people Israel knew in its own land. Yet for centuries this passage was twisted. From about the fifteenth century the curse was moved from Canaan to Ham and tied to Black Africans. Many writers and preachers used this so-called ‘curse of Ham’ to claim that God had made Africans to be slaves. In America it was preached from pulpits to defend slavery and, later, segregation. This teaching is false and evil. These notes name it and reject it. The text curses Canaan, not Ham, and it says nothing about Africa or about race.

Three verses earlier, in the same chapter, God says that every human being is made “in His own image” (9:6). No reading of Noah's words can stand against that.

If you have heard this passage used against you or your people, know that it was a lie told in God's name, and the church owes you the truth.
passages.asks: Noah's words were used for centuries to harm people God made in his image. Ask whether you have ever let a misused verse shape how you see a group of people. Then ask what it would mean to read every hard passage the way this chapter teaches: with every human life precious to God.
